question: How should the two safety chains be attached between a boat trailer and the tow vehicle?
choice_a: Left hanging loose and uncrossed, since crossing the chains serves no functional purpose
choice_b: Crisscrossed beneath the trailer coupler, and rated to support the combined weight of the boat, engine, and trailer in case the hitch separates
choice_c: Attached to only one side of the tow vehicle's hitch for a simpler connection
choice_d: Safety chains are only required on trailers longer than 30 feet
explanation: Safety chains should be crossed underneath the coupler so that, if the hitch connection fails, the crossed chains cradle the trailer tongue and keep it from dropping to the road; the chains must be strong enough to hold the combined weight of the vessel, engine, and trailer.
source_note: New Jersey Boat-Ed course, 'Trailer Safety Chains' section (boat-ed.com/newjersey)

question: What driving adjustments should an operator make while towing a boat trailer on the road?
choice_a: Drive at normal highway speeds and brake exactly as if no trailer were attached
choice_b: Take the same turning radius used when driving without a trailer
choice_c: Drive at moderate speeds, avoid sudden maneuvers, make wider turns, allow extra distance for stopping and passing, and stop periodically to check the tow vehicle, trailer, tires, and coupling
choice_d: There is no need to stop and inspect the trailer during a long tow
explanation: A loaded trailer changes a vehicle's handling, so operators should drive at moderate speeds, avoid sudden maneuvers, widen their turns, allow extra stopping and passing distance, and take periodic breaks on long trips to check the tow vehicle, trailer, tires, and coupling.
source_note: New Jersey Boat-Ed course, 'On the Road With a Trailer' section (boat-ed.com/newjersey)

question: Why should a boat operator avoid 'power loading' a boat onto its trailer using engine thrust?
choice_a: Power loading has no effect on the ramp surface or surrounding sediment
choice_b: Power loading is a required technique at all New Jersey launch ramps
choice_c: Power loading only risks damage to the tow vehicle's transmission
choice_d: Propeller wash can erode the ramp surface just beyond the ramp into a hole and deposit the eroded sediment as a mound behind it, which can trap trailer tires or ground boats
explanation: Using engine power to drive a boat onto its trailer erodes the ramp surface just past its end into a hole, while depositing the eroded material as a mound farther back; the hole can trap trailer tires and the mound can ground boats, so operators should use the winch and proper retrieval technique instead.
source_note: New Jersey Boat-Ed course, 'Do Not Power Load Your Boat' section (boat-ed.com/newjersey)

question: What should a boat operator do before beginning to fuel the boat?
choice_a: Have all passengers step onto the dock, turn off engines, fans, and anything that could spark, close all windows, ports, and doors, shut off fuel valves and open flames, and keep smoking materials away from the fueling area
choice_b: Keep passengers aboard and leave cabin windows and hatches open for ventilation
choice_c: Leave the engine and electrical equipment running to save time
choice_d: Fueling at night is always fine using an open flame for light if electric lighting isn't available
explanation: Before fueling, passengers should move to the dock, anything that could spark (engines, fans, electrical equipment) should be shut off, fuel valves and open flames such as galley stoves extinguished, windows/ports/doors closed, and no smoking or open flames allowed at the fueling area; fueling after dark should be avoided except in an emergency, and only with electric lights.
source_note: New Jersey Boat-Ed course, 'Before Fueling Your Boat' section (boat-ed.com/newjersey)

question: What precaution helps prevent a static-electricity spark while fueling a boat?
choice_a: Holding the nozzle slightly above the fill opening while pouring
choice_b: Keeping the fuel-pump nozzle in solid contact with the tank's fill opening throughout the fueling process
choice_c: Filling the tank as fast as possible to reduce the time the nozzle touches the boat
choice_d: Static electricity is not a concern when fueling a boat
explanation: Keeping the fuel-pump nozzle in solid contact with the tank opening while fueling helps prevent a static electricity discharge, which could otherwise ignite fuel vapors near the fill point.
source_note: New Jersey Boat-Ed course, 'While Fueling Your Boat' section (boat-ed.com/newjersey)

question: Why should an operator avoid filling a fuel tank all the way to the brim?
choice_a: A completely full tank makes the boat plane faster
choice_b: Fuel tanks are designed to overflow safely with no consequence
choice_c: Fuel expands with temperature changes, so room must be left in the tank to prevent it from overflowing through the vent
choice_d: There is no reason to leave room in a fuel tank
explanation: Gasoline expands as it warms, so a tank filled to the brim can overflow fuel through the vent as temperatures rise; operators should fill slowly and leave room for expansion, using an absorbent pad and wiping up any spilled fuel rather than letting it reach the bilge or water.
source_note: New Jersey Boat-Ed course, 'While Fueling Your Boat' section (boat-ed.com/newjersey)

question: After fueling and before starting the engine, what should a boat operator do?
choice_a: Start the engine immediately, since a tightly sealed fuel cap is sufficient protection
choice_b: Skip running the blower if the fueling stop took less than five minutes
choice_c: Ventilating the bilge after fueling is only necessary on boats with outboard engines
choice_d: Put the fill cap on tightly, open all windows, ports, and doors, run the power ventilation (blower) system for at least four minutes, and sniff the bilge and engine compartment for fuel vapors
explanation: After fueling, the operator should seal the fill cap tightly, reopen windows/ports/doors, run the blower for at least four minutes to clear vapors from the bilge, and sniff the bilge and engine compartment for fuel odors before starting the engine and reloading passengers, since unvented gasoline vapors settle low in the boat and can cause an explosion.
source_note: New Jersey Boat-Ed course, 'After Fueling Your Boat' section (boat-ed.com/newjersey)

question: What should a boater do to protect the trailer's electrical system just before backing the trailer down the ramp into the water?
choice_a: Disconnect the trailer's light connector from the tow vehicle so the wiring and bulbs aren't damaged by submersion
choice_b: Leave the trailer lights plugged in and switched on for underwater visibility
choice_c: Trailer light connectors are sealed and never need to be disconnected before launching
choice_d: Only disconnect the trailer lights when launching after dark
explanation: Before backing the trailer down the ramp, the trailer light connector should be disconnected from the tow vehicle to prevent the electrical connection and bulbs from being damaged when submerged during launch.
source_note: New Jersey Boat-Ed course, 'Launching Your Boat From a Trailer' section (boat-ed.com/newjersey)

question: When preparing to launch, which line should be left attached to the boat even after the tie-down straps are removed, and what additional line should be added?
choice_a: No lines are needed once the tie-down straps have been removed
choice_b: The trailer winch line should stay attached until the boat is ready to float free, and a separate rope tied to the bow lets the operator control the boat during launching
choice_c: The engine's tilt-and-trim cable should be the last connection removed before launch
choice_d: The engine kill-switch lanyard serves the same purpose as a bow control line
explanation: While preparing to launch, tie-down straps are removed but the trailer winch line should remain attached to the bow until the boat is ready to float off, and tying a separate rope to the bow gives the operator a way to control the vessel by hand during launching.
source_note: New Jersey Boat-Ed course, 'Launching Your Boat From a Trailer' section (boat-ed.com/newjersey)

question: What safety step should be taken while backing a trailer into the water to launch, before the boat is fully afloat?
choice_a: Release the tow vehicle's parking brake so it can be repositioned quickly if needed
choice_b: Wait until the boat has completely floated off the trailer before ever starting the engine
choice_c: Set the tow vehicle's parking brake, and lower and start the engine while the boat is still partly on the trailer so any starting problems are caught before it floats free
choice_d: Engine problems can always be diagnosed later back at the dock, so starting it during launch is unnecessary
explanation: While backing the trailer far enough into the water to submerge the lower unit, the tow vehicle's parking brake should be set as an added precaution, and the engine should be lowered and started while the boat is still on the trailer so that any problem can be caught while retrieval is still easy.
source_note: New Jersey Boat-Ed course, 'Backing the Trailer Into the Water During Launch' section (boat-ed.com/newjersey)

question: What is recommended for novice trailer-boat operators before attempting their first launch and retrieval at a ramp?
choice_a: Attempt backing skills for the first time at a busy public launch ramp
choice_b: Backing-up practice is unnecessary since all trailers handle identically
choice_c: Only a licensed commercial captain is permitted to back a trailer down a ramp
choice_d: Practice towing and backing up the trailer in an open field or empty parking lot beforehand
explanation: Because backing a trailer takes practice and a busy ramp is a poor place to learn, novice boaters should practice towing and backing up in an open field or empty parking lot before their first real launch and retrieval.
source_note: New Jersey Boat-Ed course, 'Backing the Trailer Into the Water During Launch' section (boat-ed.com/newjersey)
